description: The largest cluster in offshoring research pertains to global supply chains. The top cited articles in Cluster 1 address topics related to disruptions in supply chains (Blackhurst et al., 2005; Craighead et al., 2007), supply chain design (Meixell and Gargeya, 2005), and supply chain management (Bruce et al., 2004; Chan et al., 2008). Its 176 articles have been cited 9669 times, averaging 54.94 citations per article. Their average publication year is around 2011, and this cluster also is the second largest contributor in the most recent three years. Thematically, during 1989–1998, Cluster 1 encompassed themes related to global sourcing strategies (Sheth and Sharma, 1997) and importer behavior (Liang and Parkhe, 1997). In a sense, these themes represent precursors of global supply chain management literature, which emerged later. Furthermore, the themes exhibited by this cluster were dominant; Cluster 1 accounted for 13 of the total 21 publications during this decade, and it is only major cluster with publications during this time. Then in 1999–2008, the themes shifted to include supply chain severity, supply chain management (Blackhurst et al., 2005), lean and agile supply chains (Bruce et al., 2004), supply chain risks (Schoenherr et al., 2008), and global sourcing (Kotabe and Murray, 2004). That is, we find clear links between global sourcing and global supply chains. Between 2009 and 2018, we find 91 publications in Cluster 1, making it the most prolific during this period. The themes explored include global sourcing risk (Christopher et al., 2011), multi-tier supply chains (Mena et al., 2013), the role of sustainability in supplier selection (Ehrgott et al., 2011), supplier innovation (Kim and Chai, 2017), sustainable supply chains (Hsu et al., 2016), and supply chain strategy. The studies offer more in-depth assessments of global supply chains, with a focus on timely topics such as sustainability and innovation. Finally, in the past three years (2019–2021), the main focus areas have included the global supply chain during COVID-19 (Handfield et al., 2020; Remko, 2020), backshoring (Yang et al., 2021), and factors affecting supply chain strategies. Backshoring refers to relocating offshored activities to home nations (Lim and Mandrinos, 2020; Mandrinos et al., 2022). Tariffs and global supply chain complications due to the pandemic appear highly relevant, and a continued focus should address the complex implications of these disruptions, including the prominent role of unions and increased demands for better working conditions, with impacts on global supply chains. Authors also should investigate the pandemic-related supply chain crises that have plagued major economies around the world. There is already an ongoing intellectual conversation around the viability of global supply chains and GVCs and to what extent companies should rely on these connective mechanisms (Contractor, 2022). Our review suggests broad opportunities for further exploration in this cluster. In particular, two issues appear important for future research: first, future research can delve deeper into the dynamics of the optimum mix of global vs regional supply chains for offshoring firms. Second, the appropriate governance mechanisms of global supply chain relationships can be further explored.

Cluster 2 contains 149 articles, cited 9168 times, or 61.54 citations per article on average. The articles were published, on average, in 2011.40, similar to Cluster 1. The most cited articles focus on topics related to outsourcing IT services (Dibbern et al., 2008; Ellram et al., 2008; Lacity et al., 2009) and global outsourcing strategies (Ågerfalk and Fitzgerald, 2008). In terms of the publication patterns, this cluster accounts for only three publications between 1989 and 1998. Then between 1999 and 2008, its themes pertain to outsourcing software projects or workforces, sourcing strategies (Murray and Kotabe, 1999), political and cultural issues (Ang and Inkpen, 2008; Nicholson and Sahay, 2001), and new work practices in outsourcing environments. As this publication pattern reveals, outsourcing started to attract attention during this decade. The cluster publications increase in the next decade (2009–2018), when authors started exploring the influence of outsourcing on project success (Rai et al., 2009), task design and communication in business process outsourcing (Srikanth and Puranam, 2011), and risk (Nakatsu and Iacovou, 2009). A prevalent perspective centers on business process outsourcing and related strategies, which can determine project success. More recently (2019–2021), Cluster 2 has highlighted strategy-related aspects of outsourcing, including the role of culture in task performance (Presbitero, 2020), investment strategies (Pereira et al., 2021), and human resource management (Malik et al., 2021). While most research on this cluster has focused on micro-level factors such as business process characteristics, sourcing strategies, and macro-level variables, relatively less attention has been given on human issues in offshore outsourcing. For instance, importance of teamwork in offshoring projects or personality and other individual traits that facilitate the offshoring process could be further explored. Relatedly, it will be interesting to examine the vendor dynamics of IT/business process offshoring which has been neglected by the researchers. With the advent of emerging technologies such as blockchain, cloud computing, other types of artificial intelligence, it will be interesting to see how the vendors/service providers are using these digital platforms to cater to their clients.

The third largest thematic cluster focuses on outcomes, including the impact of offshoring on various economies and labor markets, which represent natural consequences of offshoring of business processes. Among the most cited articles, we find discussions of labor processes (Taylor and Bain, 2005), wealth creation (Levy, 2005), economic value creation (Farrell, 2005), declining labor incomes (Elsby et al., 2013), and changes to human resource practices in offshoring environments (Burke and Ng, 2006). Cluster 3 contains 113 articles, with 3938 citations (averaging 37.51 citations per article), and the average publication year is 2013.17, such that it is relatively recent compared with the previous two clusters. This finding is logical as well; discussions of the outcomes of offshoring naturally must follow after discussions of its processes and strategies. In terms of themes, Cluster 3 offered no publications between 1989 and 1998, but between 1999 and 2008, it produced research pertaining to the role of offshoring for economies and organizations. Furthermore, these authors discuss offshoring of both services (Gefen and Carmel, 2008; Metters and Verma, 2008) and manufacturing (Coucke and Sleuwaegen, 2008), often with a focus on the potential of such practices. In the following decade, the continued development of these discussions produced a stronger focus on the real consequences of offshoring, including declining force shares, the effects on different stakeholders (Lamin and Zaheer, 2012), location choices (Zaheer et al., 2009), and firm sustainability considerations (Dou and Sarkis, 2010). That is, the discussions moved from potential to real-world consequences, particularly in terms of the effects on the labor force of offshoring countries. Then between 2019 and 2021, we find another shift in focus, toward GVCs (Buckley et al., 2019), the nexus of offshoring and outsourcing strategies (Kaur et al., 2019), how offshoring affects R&D (García-Vega and Huergo, 2019), and job polarization (Harrigan et al., 2021; Holm et al., 2020). But discussions of the labor force in developing countries continue, and they require ongoing consideration, in terms of the effects of offshoring on labor markets in both developed and developing countries as such exploration may provide us with a more complete picture. Relatedly, the field of offshoring lacks longitudinal studies that could examine long-term effects of offshoring on firms and the business ecosystem. One reason for this scant attention is the non-availability of pertinent data at the firm and local economy levels. This suggests fertile opportunities for cross-disciplinary research in this area. A particular area where researchers can focus attention is transfer pricing. Kumar et al. (2021:275) note that transfer pricing—’the practice of pricing transactions between and within enterprises under common ownership and control (e.g., business conglomerates, multinational enterprises)—can impact a firm’s costs, revenues, and overall profitability. As firms embark on offshoring (especially captive offshoring) across locations, they need to ascertain the effect of transfer pricing on their financial outcomes. Relatedly, scholars need to empirically demonstrate how such pricing impacts the success of offshoring strategy of firms.

Cluster 4 is the last major cluster that consists of at least 100 publications. The most prominent themes, according to the most cited studies in the cluster, are talent sourcing (Manning et al., 2008), drivers of foreign investments (Nachum and Zaheer, 2005), foreign direct investments (Ramamurti, 2004), the outsourcing and offshoring nexus (Mudambi and Venzin, 2010), and offshoring of R&D (Nieto and Rodríguez, 2011). Although many of the themes are similar to those covered by Clusters 2 and 3, these articles adopt a client-side perspective. Cluster 4 contains 110 publications, which have been cited 3621 times, averaging 32.92 citations per paper. The average publication year is 2015.57, so this cluster is more recent than the previous major clusters that also comprise at least 100 publications. In this case though, we find little research (only three articles) published in the first two decades (1989–1998 and 1999–2008). But in the third decade, Cluster 4 ranked third in terms of publications, with articles that explore value creation activities in outsourcing and offshoring (Mudambi and Venzin, 2010), offshoring of R&D, commodification of labor (Bergvall-Kåreborn and Howcroft, 2014), effects of R&D outsourcing (Bertrand and Mol, 2013), and firm governance choices (Manning et al., 2018). These authors particularly highlight offshoring of research and its effect on innovation, according to factors such as knowledge management, intellectual capital, and research efforts. Governance in cross-country settings is another focus, such that authors in this cluster explore differences in the governance choices of offshoring and non-offshoring firms. Finally, between 2019 and 2021, Cluster 4 became dominant, with 27 publications. It thus represents the forefront of research in recent times. The central themes align with previous efforts, including knowledge outcomes of offshoring (Mukherjee et al., 2019) and the effects of offshore outsourcing on firm performance (Buckley et al., 2022; Munjal et al., 2019). But some new themes emerge too, such as offshoring by family businesses and small firms (Seepana et al., 2021), captive offshoring (Pongelli et al., 2019), global–local strategies adopted by offshoring firms (Malik et al., 2019), entry mode choices (Elia et al., 2019), and the effects of offshoring on pollution (Berry et al., 2021). Notably, whereas offshoring literature historically has highlighted cost savings and innovation benefits, environmental and ethical concerns have recently come to the fore. They promise the potential to encourage further research, dedicated to identifying environmental, social, and governance impacts of offshoring and how to best navigate such newer trends.

The fifth largest cluster primarily deals with determinants of offshoring, including the motivations firm have for offshoring their work tasks. The most cited articles in Cluster 5 include, as prominent topics, the use of offshoring research networks (Lewin et al., 2009; Lewin and Peeters, 2006), global strategies (Contractor et al., 2010), strategic management in IB (Doh, 2005), and internationalization by firms (Boisot and Meyer, 2008). This comparatively smaller cluster, with 49 publications, has attracted 4346 citations, for an average of 88.90 citations per article—the highest of any cluster. However, it also seems to be in a declining phase, with less interest in recent years and a publication year average of 2010.43. That is, the articles in Cluster 5 continue to inspire research (high average citation rates), but the topics covered are less popular. This finding seems logical; scholars have more or less identified all the main drivers of offshoring already. Publications in this cluster began in the 1999–2008 period, when authors explored themes such as international management, internationalization, offshoring of services, and organizational changes brought about by outsourcing and offshoring. In the effort to determine drivers of offshoring strategies, cost savings and talent acquisition came to the fore. Then during 2009–2018, authors discussed drivers in conjunction with themes such as backshoring (Kinkel and Maloca, 2009) and reshoring (Gray et al., 2013). Some attention also centered on offshoring of manufacturing and the role of value creation in offshoring decisions. Although publications rose over the past decade, we note a decline on a year-by-year basis; only two publications have appeared recently (one in 2019 and one in 2020). Those two articles described how global online platforms might enabler offshoring and the use of private branding by unaffiliated manufacturers. In a sense, it appears that the general interest has shifted, toward the influential roles of institutional actors and organizations in offshoring, as discussed by contributions assigned to the previous clusters. Nevertheless, it will be interesting for future research to study multi-level, integrative models to better specify the drivers of offshoring and provide an integrative framework for future scholars.

The smallest major thematic cluster pertains to movements of manufacturing activities, both in terms of offshoring and backshoring. Discussion of services has been ubiquitous; discussions regarding manufacturing are much more recent. The most cited articles in Cluster 6 explore themes such as manufacturing location decisions (Ellram et al., 2013), backshoring of manufacturing (Arlbjørn and Mikkelsen, 2014; Fratocchi et al., 2014; Tate, 2014), and the future of backshoring (Kinkel, 2014). This cluster contains 34 articles, cited 1403 times (an average of 41.26 citations per article). Its average publication year is 2017.09, so it is the most recent cluster; it features only one publication in the first two decades (1989–1998, 1999–2008). Instead, publications by Cluster 6 became substantial during 2009–2018, when authors addressed manufacturing location decisions. Backshoring also has gained traction, with authors exploring the challenges related to such decisions (Tate, 2014) and the factors driving them. Such efforts might represent responses to contributions that identify backshoring of manufacturing as an underresearched theme (Arlbjørn and Mikkelsen, 2014). These researchers in turn have pointed to the influences of institutional factors on location decisions (Srai and An´e, 2016). Companies’ decisions to reshore manufacturing to high-cost home countries have prompted some authors to consider factors other than location-related costs (Gray et al., 2017), as well as the process and strategies used to achieve such reshoring (McIvor and Bals, 2021). In the past three years, scholars have continued to explore such topics, such as behavioral factors related to location decisions (Pla-Barber et al., 2019), but also related notions, such as the relationship between the adoption of industry 4.0 and backshoring decisions (Ancarani et al., 2019; Dachs et al., 2019). This relatively new frontier of research has great potential for growth. Many questions remain to be explored, including the roles of factors such as reputational risk, the host country’s image, and institutional changes in offshoring and reshoring decisions related to manufacturing vs. service activities.
